claims.text: Containerless electromagnetic levitation combined with in-situ high-speed pyrometry and synchrotron diffraction yields accurate and efficient melting-property measurements for high-entropy alloys.
The proposed approach determines melting temperature more accurately than, or at least consistently with, conventional DSC.
The proposed approach can determine enthalpy of fusion.
The proposed approach can determine entropy of fusion.
The proposed approach can determine volume change at melting.
The proposed approach can determine liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
Ultra-high vacuum minimizes contamination and oxidation during levitation melting.
Electromagnetic levitation avoids contact between the molten alloy and a crucible.
Removing container-induced heterogeneities produces a more intrinsic liquid-phase structure.
The more intrinsic liquid structure better reflects the true thermodynamic state through volume changes and diffraction signatures.
Conventional DSC can be affected by contamination, crucible interactions, heterogeneous nucleation, thermal lag, and slower response.
Containerless processing avoids contamination and heterogeneous nucleation effects associated with conventional DSC.
In-situ high-speed pyrometry precisely captures thermal evolution during melting and cooling.
High-speed synchrotron diffraction monitors structural changes during melting.
Combined pyrometry and diffraction permit rapid, high-resolution tracking of energy absorption, disorder increment, and volume change without container reactions or thermal lag.
Reduced measurement uncertainty should be observable across a broad range of high-entropy-alloy compositions.
The method is applicable where evaporation losses and chemical reactivity do not compromise droplet stability.
Alloys containing very high-vapor-pressure or highly reactive elements may require additional process control.
Fusion enthalpy and entropy can be extracted from calibrated temperature-time profiles.
Volume changes at melting can be inferred from synchrotron diffraction patterns.
